title: Al-Hafiz, the Preserver
hookLine: the Preserver, who guards all things
tomorrow: food keeps appearing, and nobody brought it. where's it from?

lines: A FATHER LETS HIS SON GO.
cards: The airport curb, right after the hug. You watch them walk toward security until the crowd swallows them, and then you stand there a second longer, as if looking could keep them safe.
Yesterday's question: who guards the people you love when you can't? In the Qur'an, a father faces that exact moment. Ya'qub has already lost one son.
Now his other sons want to take the youngest on the road. And he says: Allah is better at guarding.

teach.b: That's Al-Hafiz, the Preserver, who guards all things. The Throne Verse says it of the heavens and the earth, in Pickthall's words: "He is never weary of preserving them." Never weary.
No refreshing needed. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight.
In a hadith the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught a boy, he said: be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you. In Arabic, mindful and protect are the same verb, hafiza.
Guard Him in your life, and you are guarded.
Now the week, coming back. The Forbearing: three seconds slower than the room. The Magnificent: everything finds its size.

teach.h: YOUR PART: THE DU'A AND THE TEXT.
teach.b: The All-Forgiving: He covers. The Appreciative: nothing is too small. The Most High: the heavy thing goes on the floor.
The Most Great: greater, with nothing after. And today, the one who keeps all of it, and all of them. Ya'qub still let his son go, and still told them to be careful.
Guarding the people you love belongs first to the Preserver; your part is the du'a and the text that says, get home safe.

how: Muslims ask Allah, al-Hafiz, to protect those they love, often with du'a for travelers; some recite the Throne Verse (2:255) before a journey and before sleep.

o: the Preserver, who guards all things
the one who guards only the faithful
the one who prevents every bad thing

games.q: two weeks of Names — tap the pairs.
p: the heavy thing goes on the floor

s: trusting Allah to guard someone means you never warn them to be careful
Ya'qub said Allah is better at guarding, and still sent his sons off with advice.
in the hadith, 'be mindful of Allah' and 'He will protect you' use the same verb
ihfaz Allah, yahfazka: guard Him, and you are guarded.

games.q: your mom is flying overseas tonight and you can't sleep. you've checked the flight tracker for the tenth time. what fits Al-Hafiz?
o: keep checking; if you stop watching, you're not really caring.
send her one line, make a du'a if you pray, and set the phone down.
don't think about her at all; worrying shows you don't trust God.
games.why: the Preserver is never weary of guarding. your part is the line and the du'a; the watching belongs to Him.

practice: Choose one person you love who's on the road, in a hard week, or far away. Send them one short line that asks nothing back: thinking of you, get home safe.
Some say a du'a for them by name as it sends; either way, let the sit be the moment you hand them over.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hafiz. The Preserver, who guards all things and is never weary of it.

orig.note: Arabic: the Preserver, the Guardian. from the verb in 'be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you'.

carryVoice: Keep this: preserved, the people you love included, even when your phone shows nothing. That's two weeks of Names, held.

sources.q: He is never weary of preserving them.

sources.ref: Qur'an 12:63–67 (Ya'qub: Allah is better at guarding; his advice to his sons)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2516; al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in 19 (be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you)
